lessons.title: Tools and equipment for planting
lessons.html:
Getting ready to plant

Planting is one of the most important jobs on the farm. If plants are put in the ground badly, the whole crop suffers. You will plant under the guidance of your supervisor, who tells you what to plant, where and how.

Common planting tools

ToolUse
Spade or hoeDig holes and loosen soil
Planting stick or dibberMake holes for seedlings or seed
Measuring tape, marked stick, line and pegsMeasure spacing between rows and plants
RakeLevel the seedbed and cover seed
Watering can or hoseWater after planting
Wheelbarrow and seedling traysCarry plants to the land
Hand planter or jab planterPlant seed such as maize or beans by hand

Big farms use tractor planters and transplanters. You may help by filling seed boxes, checking that seed falls, or feeding seedlings into a transplanter.

Before you go to the land, check with your supervisor which tools are needed for the crop. Take enough for your team and some spare string and pegs.

Using tools safely

  • Check tools before use. Report loose heads or broken handles.
  • Carry spades and hoes with the blade down.
  • Keep a safe space between you and the next worker.
  • Wear boots, a hat and gloves.
  • Bend your knees, not your back, when lifting trays.
  • Stay away from moving tractors and planters.

Caring for tools

  • Knock off soil after use and wash tools if needed.
  • Dry them so they do not rust. Oil metal parts sometimes.
  • Keep blades sharp.
  • Return tools to the store and hang them up.
  • Clean tools that may carry disease before moving to another land, if told.

lessons.title: Handling planting material
lessons.html:
Planting material is alive

Planting material can be seed, seedlings, cuttings, tubers (like seed potatoes) or bulbs. All of these are alive and must be handled gently.

Seed

  • Keep seed in a cool, dry place, away from rats and insects.
  • Many seeds are treated with chemicals and are coloured (for example pink or red maize seed). Never eat treated seed or give it to animals. Wear gloves and wash your hands after handling it.
  • Check the seed bag label for the crop, variety and lot number.
  • Do not mix different varieties.

Seedlings

Seedlings of cabbage, tomato, onion, peppers and many other crops come from a nursery in trays.

  • Water the trays well before planting so the plugs come out easily.
  • Keep trays in the shade until planting.
  • Take out seedlings by holding the leaves or the soil plug, never by the thin stem. A crushed stem kills the plant.
  • Plant only healthy seedlings. Put aside yellow, weak or sick ones and show your supervisor.
  • Plant on the same day they arrive if possible.

Cuttings and tubers

  • Keep cuttings moist and shaded.
  • Plant cuttings the right way up, with buds pointing up.
  • Handle seed potatoes gently so sprouts do not break off.

How the environment affects the crop

  • Temperature: seeds need warm soil to grow. Planting too early in cold soil gives poor germination. Frost kills many young plants.
  • Water: seeds need moist soil to sprout. Seedlings need water straight after planting.
  • Sun: hot sun and wind dry out new plants fast. Plant in the cool morning or late afternoon if possible.
  • Soil: loose, fine soil helps roots grow. Hard or lumpy soil gives poor growth.
  • Wind: strong wind breaks and dries out seedlings.

lessons.title: Planting at the right spacing and depth
lessons.html:
Why spacing matters

Each plant needs space for its roots and leaves. If plants are too close, they fight for water, light and food, and you get many small plants. If they are too far apart, land is wasted and weeds grow in the gaps. Your supervisor will give you the spacing for the crop.

Example spacings (your farm may differ)

CropBetween rowsBetween plants
Cabbageabout 60 cmabout 40 to 50 cm
Tomatoesabout 1 to 1.5 mabout 50 cm
Onionsabout 30 cmabout 8 to 10 cm

Marking out

  1. Stretch a line tight between two pegs to mark a straight row.
  2. Measure the row spacing with a tape or marked stick.
  3. Mark plant positions with a marked stick laid along the row.

Planting depth

  • Seed: a common rule is to plant about two to three times as deep as the seed is wide. Small seeds go shallow; big seeds like maize and beans go deeper. Follow your supervisor's depth.
  • Seedlings: plant so the top of the soil plug is just covered, at the same depth as in the tray. Some crops, like tomatoes, may be planted a little deeper; your supervisor will say.
  • Too deep: seed may not come up. Too shallow: seed dries out or birds eat it.

Planting steps for seedlings

  1. Make a hole at the marked place, a bit bigger than the plug.
  2. Put the seedling in, upright.
  3. Press soil firmly around it so there are no air pockets.
  4. Water straight away.
  5. Check your row: straight, correct spacing, no missed places.

After planting, report empty places and dead plants so they can be replanted.

Key points

  • Use tools safely and return them clean.
  • Never eat treated seed; wash hands after handling it.
  • Hold seedlings by the leaves or plug, never the stem.
  • Plant at the spacing and depth your supervisor gives.
  • Firm the soil and water straight after planting.
